lessons.title: Materials and their properties
lessons.programRef: MINEDUB primary school curriculum (English-speaking subsystem), Level III — Elementary Science and Technology; to be checked against the official texts
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Name common materials and their properties.
Choose a suitable material for a job and give the reason.
Tell natural from man-made materials and reversible from irreversible changes.
reviewNotes: Rusting and egg cooking are given as irreversible changes (standard examples). Floating/sinking and density are intentionally left out.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Materials
blocks.md: Everything is made of **materials**. **Natural** materials come from plants, animals or the earth: wood, cotton, wool, leather, clay, stone. **Man-made** materials are made by people: plastic, glass, nylon, cement. Every material has **properties**: hard or soft, rigid or flexible, strong or weak, rough or smooth, waterproof or absorbent, transparent or opaque, conductor or insulator, magnetic or not.

blocks.caption: Common materials and one property of each.
blocks.alt: Six boxes: wood is hard and burns, metal conducts heat, plastic is waterproof, glass is transparent, cloth is soft and flexible and rubber stretches.

blocks.title: Choosing a material
blocks.md: Ask: what must the object **do**? Then pick the material with the right property. An umbrella needs a **waterproof** cover. A window needs **transparent** glass. A cooking pot needs a **conductor** of heat (metal), but its handle needs an **insulator** (wood or plastic). A towel needs an **absorbent** cloth.

blocks.title: Changes in materials
blocks.md: In a **reversible** change the material can come back: ice melts to water and water freezes to ice. In an **irreversible** change a **new** material is made and we cannot go back: burning wood, cooking an egg, rusting iron, baking a cake. Heating, cooling and mixing can all cause changes.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Giving a reason that does not match the job (a window made of wood because wood is strong, when we need to see through it).
- Thinking that all plastics are the same: they differ in strength and flexibility.
- Saying that melting wax is irreversible: it can go solid again when it cools, so it is reversible.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Which material is best for the handle of a kettle: metal, wood or glass? Give a reason.
steps: The handle must not let the heat pass, so we need an insulator.
Wood (or plastic) is an insulator; metal is a conductor.
blocks.answer: Wood (or plastic), because it is an insulator and stays cool.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: Say whether each change is reversible or irreversible: (a) ice melting, (b) wood burning.
steps: (a) Water can freeze again into ice: reversible.
(b) Burning wood makes ash and smoke, new materials: irreversible.

lessons.title: Protecting the environment: pollution and waste
lessons.programRef: MINEDUB primary school curriculum (English-speaking subsystem), Level III — Elementary Science and Technology; to be checked against the official texts
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Name the kinds of pollution and give their causes and effects.
Use the three Rs: reduce, reuse and recycle.
Say how to manage waste and protect trees, water and soil.
reviewNotes: Statements that plastic 'does not rot easily' are kept general. Local rules on waste (burning, sorting) differ; to be checked by the school or a health worker.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Pollution
blocks.md: **Pollution** is adding harmful things to the air, water or soil. **Air pollution**: smoke from burning rubbish, old vehicles and factories. **Water pollution**: rubbish, oil, soap or chemicals in rivers and streams. **Soil pollution**: dumped waste, plastic and chemicals. **Noise pollution**: very loud sounds. Pollution harms people (coughs, stomach illnesses), animals and plants.

items.text: Buy less. Use again. Make into new things.

blocks.caption: The three Rs: reduce, reuse, recycle.
blocks.alt: Three boxes joined by arrows: Reduce, Reuse and Recycle. A line of text says buy less, use again, make into new things.

blocks.title: Managing waste
blocks.md: **Biodegradable** waste rots and goes back to the soil (food scraps, leaves, paper, banana peel). Put it in a compost heap. **Non-biodegradable** waste does not rot easily (plastic bags, bottles, tins). **Reduce** what you throw away, **reuse** bottles and bags, **recycle** where possible. Put rubbish in bins and never in drains or rivers: blocked drains cause floods and breed mosquitoes.

blocks.title: Protecting nature
blocks.md: Plant trees: they give shade, food and oxygen, hold the soil and give homes to animals. **Deforestation** (cutting trees without planting) causes erosion and destroys habitats. Save water: close the tap, collect rain, do not waste. Keep rivers and the school compound clean. Washing hands after handling rubbish keeps us healthy.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Burning plastic: it makes poisonous smoke.
- Throwing rubbish into drains or streams, thinking that the rain will carry it away.
- Thinking that one person cannot help: a clean school compound begins with each pupil.
- Mixing biodegradable and non-biodegradable waste in one heap.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Sort into biodegradable and non-biodegradable: banana peel, plastic bag, dry leaves, tin.
steps: Banana peel and dry leaves rot in the soil: biodegradable.
A plastic bag and a tin do not rot easily: non-biodegradable.
blocks.answer: Biodegradable: banana peel, dry leaves. Non-biodegradable: plastic bag, tin.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: A school wants to reduce its waste. Give three ideas using the three Rs.
steps: Reduce: use both sides of the paper.
Reuse: refill water bottles and use cloth bags.
Recycle: make compost from leaves and food scraps.
blocks.answer: Use both sides of paper (reduce), refill bottles (reuse) and compost leaves (recycle).
